visible.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex activity carries up to 2 years under Article 338 — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Indecency-law application to trans people is documented in aggregate, not per-case; tourism volume is very low.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country page (Algeria): NGOs document arrests within the LGBT+ community with little information on the trans identity of those arrested; no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare — arts. 274/264 could be used against providers (de facto criminalisation); no legal gender-recognition route, so civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked.

UK Home Office CPIN 'Algeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression' (26 Jul 2026, covering since May 2025): same-sex activity prohibited under Penal Code 1966 ('acts of homosexuality', Human Dignity Trust updated June 2026); internal relocation viable for gay males but lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties; refusals rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded — the current asylum-authority baseline.

Snopes fact-check (5 Aug 2024): Rating TRUE — Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and being transgender; published while debunking the false Imane Khelif 'trans boxer' rumour, confirming the ban is real even though the rumour about the athlete was false.

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Algeria): law criminalised undefined 'homosexual acts' with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment plus fines; prison authorities separated vulnerable persons but LGBTQI+ detainees had no specific legal protections; civil society noted compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons.

ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia 2008: Algeria — male/male and female/female relations illegal under Penal Code (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966): 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. Dated but the same Penal Code 1966 that the 2026 CPIN confirms is still in force.

Human Rights Watch (15 Oct 2020): after a 24 Jul 2020 raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, police arrested 44 people (9 women, 35 men, mostly university students) over an alleged 'gay wedding'; on 3 Sep 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and 42 to suspended terms, using decorations and 'gay appearance' as evidence.

BBC/Arab Barometer (23 Jun 2019, 25,000 respondents across 10 countries + Palestinian territories): Algeria was the exception where fewer than 50% accepted a woman head of state; region-wide, 'not religious' identification rose from 8% to 13% since 2013 — social-conservatism context datum for the record.

visible.summary:
Tunisia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the 2024-25 arrest wave explicitly included trans women on gender-identity grounds.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.

sources.claim: Amnesty International (11 Feb 2025): at least 84 people — mainly gay men and trans women — arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef between 26 Sep 2024 and 31 Jan 2025 on 'public indecency'/morality charges; a 31 Oct 2024 mass conviction drew prison terms up to 4.5 years, upheld on appeal 5 Feb 2025 (four released after reduction). Quantified 2024-25 crackdown evidence.

Cairo 52 country page: Penal Code Article 230 criminalises same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' imprisonment; records enforcement (e.g. Oct 2021 arrest of two transgender women under morality/debauchery provisions) and gaps in legal gender recognition. Primary-law summary for visitor risk.

Intersection Association (Nov 2024): transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings — systemic identity refusal from detention onward, described as continuous suffering and discrimination inside the prison system. Direct trans-specific custodial-risk evidence.

Cairo 52 (30 Jan 2024): reports the Tunis Court of First Instance's Apr 2023 refusal of legal gender recognition to a transgender man; the court weighed contradictory lower-court judgements (incl. case No. 12304/2018) and found no consistent precedent, leaving recognition unsettled below the Court of Cassation. Shows LGR is court-by-court and often denied.

Human Rights Watch (29 Mar 2016): documents at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months, all convicted under Penal Code art. 230 (up to 3 years); interviewed detainees reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police. Core enforcement-abuse evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 Sep 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases, but kept the anti-gay law itself; Kapitalis warns the pledge does not decriminalise anything. Shows reform-by-commitment without legal change.

visible.summary:
Cameroon is dangerous for trans visitors. The Shakiro case is the defining documentation: in February 2021, trans women Shakiro and Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing, convicted of “attempted homosexuality,” “indecent dressing” and ID irregularities, and sentenced to five years. They described five months of “hell” in Douala's central prison, initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; Shakiro later received asylum in Belgium. Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years), and Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates.

Police and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and there is no legal gender recognition or protection of any kind. The Shakiro conviction shows that visible trans expression in a public place is itself treated as a prosecutable offence.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation in public risks arrest on indecency/ID grounds; prison conditions are severe.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years) — the vehicle for the Shakiro convictions and a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; the Shakiro case demonstrates direct application to gender expression.

sources.claim: BBC (12 May 2021): Douala court jailed trans woman Shakiro (YouTuber) and friend Patricia for five years under 'attempted homosexuality' plus 200,000 CFA francs ($370) each — the maximum statutory term — with appeal filed; detained since February 2021. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called it a political decision with no proof of acts. Notes Cameroon's 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, one of 31 African countries criminalising, with beatings of gay/trans people common in public.

Wikipedia biography of Shakiro (b. 29 July 1997, Douala): Cameroonian trans activist who gained Facebook/YouTube following discussing trans life; arrested and charged with 'attempted homosexuality' in 2021, sentenced to five years, subsequently fled Cameroon and claimed asylum abroad. Serves as biographical corroboration of the 2021 case and its outcome (exile), tracking the human-rights profile of the criminalisation cases.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Cameroon: documents discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prisons, and arbitrary arrests - the criminalisation context (Article 347).

Human Rights Watch (11 May 2022): documented a 2022 uptick of violence against LGBTI people — since 9 March, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least 6 and detained 11 people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; gendarmes beat two in detention. Frames the pattern: the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence, per HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi.

CNN (9 Jan 2013): Cameroon appeals court acquitted Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, jailed five years in November 2011 solely because they wore women's clothes and ordered Baileys — the original judge had cited dress, speech and the drink as proof they were gay. Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts (lawyer Alice Nkom, All Out petition; Amnesty welcomed the acquittal). Establishes the pattern: arrests on effeminacy/appearance grounds under colonial-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.

visible.summary:
Tanzania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex activity criminalised with up to life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the Mauzinde attack is trans-specific.

sources.claim: JURIST (9 Jun 2024): UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo — abducted by 12 men, found beaten in a forest with her ears cut — calling for 'bold action to combat discrimination against #LGBTIQ+ people'; the UN flagged possible violations of ICCPR Art. 20 and Tanzania's Constitution Art. 13 equality guarantees.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Tanzania's criminalisation of same-sex activity (life imprisonment possible).

OONI report 'Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship' (2024, PDF): documents the blocking of LGBTIQ websites and other targeted blocks in Tanzania based on OONI measurement data — including LGBTIQ social networks and rights sites — evidencing state-directed online filtering that constrains LGBT access to information.

Amnesty International report (Jan 2024, AFR 01/75/33/2024, 'We Are Facing Extinction'): documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment — national-level findings.

Interview (Rainer Ebert, 4 Sep 2020) with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists: documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy; includes definitions of sexual orientation, gender identity and trans woman terms.

Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 (full text, PDF): enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives; defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute under 12; under-18 and marriage distinctions) and penalties including imprisonment for three years — Zanzibar-specific criminal law applying to the semi-autonomous islands alongside mainland law.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania: the three most widespread problems were security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice; also 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' and societal violence against persons with albinism.

visible.summary:
Ethiopia is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than Cameroon's or Tunisia's — Ethiopia's LGBTQ+ community (self-identified as “zega”) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation + no LGR catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it clearly on the dangerous side of the scale. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the UPR reporting.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex criminalisation (up to 1 year, more under aggravation) — because there is no LGR, a trans person's relationships are legally same-sex; a direct mechanism, not merely climate.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.

sources.claim: Stakeholder submission to Ethiopia's UPR (47th session): same-sex activity criminalised, leaving LGBTQ+ people at serious risk of harm and systematic exclusion; discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services; no legal gender change - trans men are legally women and trans women legally men, so trans people in different-gender relationships can fall foul of the same-sex conduct law.

Stakeholder UPR report by The Advocates for Human Rights and House of Guramayle (April 2024) on SOGIE in Ethiopia: documents discrimination, violence, and lack of protection; notes transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework.

F&M Global Barometers country profile, time series 2011-2024 (all years scored 'no' on every protection axis): no legal gender recognition (neither surgical nor psychiatric pathway exists), no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no freedom from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity/expression, LGBTI organisations cannot register, Pride events not allowed and participants unprotected, no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protections including gender identity. National LGBTI organisations exist despite the ban on registration.
US State Department 2008 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma - baseline country-of-origin information.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents arrests of opposition figures, CSO-law restrictions on civil society, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia: documents the anti-terrorism prosecutions, CSO-law restrictions, torture, harsh prisons - general context with the LGBT section noting criminalisation.

Lund University master's thesis (2009) by Daniel Iddo Balcha: 'Homosexuality in Ethiopia' - analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender and feminism; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elite create homophobia in discourse; the church effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code outlaws same-sex conduct between men and between women — rarely enforced but underpinning pervasive anti-LGBTIQ stigma, harassment and violence; in August 2023 security forces cracked down on 'homosexuality' while non-state actors drove an online incitement wave ending in physical attacks; Christian and Muslim groups campaign for harsher penalties (Orthodox Church declared its stance June 2024). Charities & Societies Proclamation Art 69 blocks registration of LGBTI groups as 'contrary to public morality'. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI orgs cannot register.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Ethiopia §6.7: criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct drives near-total concealment of identity — individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+; activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, with harassment/violence increasing toward end of 2023. High levels of societal discrimination nationwide in education, employment and healthcare; being outed risks physical violence and ostracism. Authoritative annual baseline for state and social risk to a trans visitor.

visible.summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 534 ("intercourse contrary to the order of nature," up to 1 year) — a situational risk for trans visitors with partners, though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations.
visible.localsOnly: The case-by-case post-surgery LGR rulings and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR case law and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing; Art 521/534 are the traveler-relevant statutes.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review: Lebanon employs both de facto and explicit criminalisation to penalise transgender expression, particularly targeting transgender women; a rise in prejudice and violence against trans and queer people is documented in Beirut, including incidents responding to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament; gradual legal-gender-recognition progress since 2015 when a judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents.

EUAA Country Focus Lebanon sec. 7.5 (fetched 2026-09-29): dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons including activists in the asylum country-of-origin report — treats LGBTIQ claims as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and source methodology.

HRW (8 Apr 2022, Nora Noralla): regional dispatch 'Tough Territory for Transgender People' — Egypt, Lebanon and Tunisia should ensure access to legal gender recognition; documents trans people's exposure to policing and documentation barriers in Lebanon alongside neighbours.

Manara Magazine (Mar 2022, Nora Noralla): maps MENA case law on legal gender recognition — the Lebanese judiciary has a long history of reviewing trans plaintiffs' name/marker changes governed by the civil registry code of 1951, with an 1887-era... [Lebanese Civil Decision 1987] precedent and heavy roles for medical and religious authorities; compares Lebanon with Egypt, Kuwait and UAE reasoning.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026), at-a-glance: same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country; legal gender recognition not possible (overview page cached truncated at ~5KB; article-level detail on Art. 534 not retrievable in cache).

HRW (18 May 2018): security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride — nine days of LGBT-identity activities — in a crackdown HRW called a violation of freedom of assembly and a step backward for LGBT rights.

The Daily Beast (15 May 2018): profile of Georges Azzi, who co-founded Helem in 2004 (the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world) and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile regional countries.

HRW (2 Feb 2017): 'Another Judge Questions Legal Basis of Prosecuting Homosexivity Under Lebanese Law' — a ruling pushed Lebanon closer to decriminalising same-sex conduct, following the 2009 precedent that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence.
